title: The daughters
hook: Montaigne lost five of six daughters in infancy and wrote little of it, which readers still wonder about

segments.voice: Yesterday, of experience: the last essay, where Montaigne learns most from his own plain life. Your line was ordinary lessons. What did yesterday teach you that no book did? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

Here is a man who tells you about his kidney stones, his digestion, his bad memory, how he likes his meat cooked and how long he likes to sleep. Nothing seems too small or too private for his book. And then, in one sentence, tucked inside an argument about something else, he mentions that some of his children died as babies. One sentence. Then he moves on. Readers have stopped at that sentence for a long time and asked what's underneath it. Today is about that silence.
screen: `KIDNEY STONES, MEAT, MEMORY.` → `ONE SENTENCE ABOUT HIS CHILDREN.` → `THEN HE MOVES ON.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence itself. In an early essay, Montaigne is arguing that much of what hurts us hurts because of the opinion we hold about it. As an example, he says he has lost two or three children while they were still nursing, not without regret, but without great grief. That's all. Second, what sits around it. The same writer gave a whole essay to his friend Étienne de La Boétie, and to losing him. Asked why he loved him, Montaigne says it could only be answered: because it was he, because it was I. So he could write grief, openly and at length. Here he doesn't. Third, how readers take the silence. Some take him at his word: this was his honest report, in a time and place that spoke of such losses differently. Some hear a man using his own argument as armor, saying the calm thing because the true thing was too heavy for the page. Some simply notice that he doesn't give the number exactly, two or three, and they sit with that. Nobody can open the inside of another person's grief, and Montaigne doesn't open this one for us. Fourth, why this matters outside the book. The man next to you on the train, the coworker who laughs easily, the grandmother who never mentions the brother she lost. Some grief gets whole pages. Some gets one sentence and a closed door. Both are real. The quiet kind just asks for gentler eyes.
screen: `TWO OR THREE, WHILE NURSING.` · `PAGES FOR HIS FRIEND.` · `HONEST CALM, OR ARMOR?` · `SOME GRIEF GETS ONE SENTENCE.` · then, large: `HIDDEN GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think gently of a hidden grief. Sit, and let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind a grief that doesn't get talked about. It can be someone else's, a person you know who carries a loss quietly. Or it can be your own, if that feels safe today. You don't need to open it or explain it. Just turn toward it the way you'd sit beside someone on a bench without asking questions. Let the breath be soft around it. The bell holds the time.
The daughters. Montaigne wrote one passing sentence about losing children in infancy, and readers still wonder what that short sentence holds back. Today's word.
Your line: hidden grief. Today, be a little gentler with one quiet person, without asking them to explain anything. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often pause at his one passing remark about losing children in infancy and read it in more than one way: as an honest report, or as grief held back from the page.

fork.setup: you're reading Montaigne and reach his one sentence about the children he lost. what does the script say readers do with it?
options: read it in more than one way, and admit no one can open his grief for him.
fork.reveal: readers differ: an honest report, an argument used as armor, or a number he couldn't even give exactly. Montaigne doesn't open it for us.

trapdoor: what you thought: if he wrote so little, it didn't matter much to him.
what it means: one sentence can carry a grief its writer chooses not to open.
what a scholar hears: the remark sits inside an essay arguing that pain depends partly on our opinion of it, which is why some readers wonder whether the argument shaped the calm.

sources.ref: Essays 1.14 (numbered 1.40 in some editions), That the taste of good and evil depends in large part on our opinion of them (he has lost two or three children at nurse, not without regret but without great grief)

notes: The index hook says Montaigne lost five of six daughters in infancy. Under the claims rule the script does not state that count, because the Essays do not; it uses only Montaigne's own 'two or three' (Essays 1.14 / 1.40). The index hook should be checked against the biographical record (the family calendar) before release.
The script does not mention his surviving daughter Léonor, to avoid an unsourced count; a scholar may want her named.
'Because it was he, because it was I' is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the essay number (1.28 in the usual modern numbering, 1.27 in some editions).
The three readings of the silence are offered without ranking; confirm they are fair to the scholarship.
The hook's list (kidney stones, digestion, memory, meat, sleep) draws on Essays 2.17, 2.37 and 3.13; confirm each detail.

Editor pass: 'whole pages to the death of' La Boétie changed to 'a whole essay to his friend, and to losing him' (the death account itself is in a letter, not 1.28); 'couldn't even give the number' softened to 'doesn't give'; varied the 'ordinary day' turn.
